title: Americans Support Price Shopping For Health Care, But Few Actually Seek Out Price Information
abstract: The growing awareness of the wide variation in health care prices, increased availability of price data, and increased patient cost sharing are expected to drive patients to shop for lower-cost medical services. We conducted a nationally representative survey of 2,996 nonelderly US adults who had received medical care in the previous twelve months to assess how frequently patients are price shopping for care and the barriers they face in doing so. Only 13 percent of respondents who had some out-of-pocket spending in their last health care encounter had sought information about their expected spending before receiving care, and just 3 percent had compared costs across providers before receiving care. The low rates of price shopping do not appear to be driven by opposition to the idea: The majority of respondents believed that price shopping for care is important and did not believe that higher-cost providers were of higher quality. Common barriers to shopping included difficulty obtaining price information and a desire not to disrupt existing provider relationships.

Americans Support Price Shopping For Health Care, But Few Actually Seek Out Price Information (2017) in Health Affairs. Top 1% most-cited for its field and year.

Full narrative

Americans Support Price Shopping For Health Care, But Few Actually Seek Out Price Information (2017) in Health Affairs is authored by Ateev Mehrotra, Katie Dean and Anna D. Sinaiko. Topics: Health care, Opposition (politics), Business, Health care cost and Quality (philosophy).

72 citations (OpenAlex). Citations peaked in 2019 with 16 citing works. Citing venues include JAMA Network Open, Health Services Research and Journal of Hospital Medicine.

Limited online visibility beyond citations.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This Health Affairs article has drawn substantial scholarly attention, with 72 citations and field-normalized standing in the top 1% for its year. Its reach is concentrated in policy and health services research venues, and the citation record suggests the paper became a reference point for later work on price transparency, cost sharing, and patient shopping behavior in health care.

Full narrative

Mehrotra, Dean, Sinaiko, and Sood asked a timely and policy-relevant question: although patients often say they support price shopping for health care, how many actually seek out price information when they receive care? Using a nationally representative survey of 2,996 nonelderly US adults who had received medical care in the prior year, the study showed that price shopping was uncommon, and it identified practical barriers that help explain why the promise of transparency does not automatically translate into consumer behavior.

The article’s scholarly footprint is strong. OpenAlex records 72 citations, placing it in the top 1% of papers for its field and publication year. Those citations are spread across a sustained run of follow-on publications rather than a single burst, with especially visible uptake in venues such as JAMA Network Open, Health Services Research, Journal of Hospital Medicine, Annals of Internal Medicine, and Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research. That pattern indicates that the paper has been used widely in discussions of health care pricing and patient decision-making.

The citing literature is also methodologically and topically aligned with the original study. Most citing works are journal articles, and the dominant concepts center on health care policy and management, health care cost and quality, health systems, and patient satisfaction. Recent citing papers continue to use the article as part of a broader conversation about transparency policies, reference pricing, low-cost provider use, and price dispersion, including work on MRI markets, prescription benefit tools, and systematic reviews of price transparency outcomes.

Beyond citations, the record shows additional downstream reuse: 73 documented reuse instances, including reviews, preprints, a report, and a book chapter. Scite also shows mostly mentioning citations with a small number of supporting statements, which is consistent with a paper that is frequently invoked as background evidence and occasionally used to substantiate claims about the limits of consumer price shopping. Public-facing attention appears modest rather than broad: the record includes one general-audience blog mention, while other media signals are sparse. Overall, the article has become an influential empirical anchor in debates over price transparency, even as the evidence base suggests that information alone is not enough to make most patients active price shoppers.
